statements.text: I'm concerned about the ramifications of the accessible AI tools to improve our adversaries' cyber capabilities. What should we be most concerned about regarding Iran's use of AI?
statements.context: House committee hearing on Iranian regime threats to homeland security, during a member's questioning period.

statements.text: How do you share information with CISA currently? What would the best structure for JCDC.AI, what would that look like?
statements.context: House Homeland Security Committee hearing on DHS and CISA roles in securing AI, where a member questions a witness about CISA's AI threat-intelligence sharing plans.

statements.text: CISA's information-sharing mission is crucial. Do you think CISA has the tools it needs to be able to notify entities of potential AI threats? Is CISA's ability to issue administrative subpoenas sufficient?
statements.context: House Homeland Security Committee hearing examining DHS and CISA roles in AI security.

statements.text: Today, we have four expert witnesses who will help shed light on the potential risks related to the use of AI in critical infrastructure, including how AI may enable malicious cyber actors' offensive attacks, but also how AI may enable defensive cyber tools for threat detection, prevention, and vulnerability assessments.
statements.context: Opening statement by the subcommittee chair at a congressional hearing on DHS and CISA's role in securing AI, held December 12, 2023.

statements.text: Last, Mr. Swanson, how do you expect malicious actors will leverage AI to carry out cyber attacks? Do you think the efforts to use AI for cyber defense—and do you think the efforts to use AI for cyber defense will progress faster than efforts to use AI for offensive cyber operations?
statements.context: House hearing on DHS and CISA roles in AI security, questioning a witness about offensive and defensive cyber uses of AI.

statements.text: Mr. O'Neill, I'm concerned about the use of AI further exacerbating the risk associated with the interdependencies across critical infrastructure sectors. Does your sector understand the risk associated with these interdependencies in AI? What are you doing to mitigate that risk? Is there more that CISA can do to help?
statements.context: House Homeland Security Committee hearing examining DHS and CISA roles in securing AI, featuring a member questioning a witness on infrastructure risk.

statements.text: I understand the AI EO placed a heavy emphasis on the usage of the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, including a requirement for DHS to incorporate the Framework into relevant guidelines for critical infrastructure owners and operators. [...] Do you think the EO strikes the right balance of the breakdown of responsibility between DHS and CISA? [...] how should CISA support critical infrastructure to protect against malicious use of small and open-source models?
statements.context: Written questions submitted by House Subcommittee Chairman Garbarino to witnesses after a hearing on DHS and CISA's role in securing AI.

statements.text: The EO directs DHS to establish an Artificial Intelligence Safety and Security Board. How can the Secretary best scope the composition and mission of the board? What kind of perspectives do you think the DHS should ensure are represented?
statements.context: House committee hearing on DHS and CISA roles in AI security.

statements.text: Ms. Moore, Mr. O'Neill brought up red-teaming in one of his answers before, and I understand CISA is tasked in the Executive Order with supporting red-teaming for generative AI.
statements.context: House committee hearing on DHS and CISA roles in securing AI, where Rep. Garbarino questions a witness about CISA's red-teaming mandate.

statements.text: The purpose of this hearing is to provide an opportunity to hear from private industry on how the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) can support efforts to secure artificial intelligence (AI) and how the use of AI will impact cybersecurity. [...] one that may make this conversation much more challenging is the creation of machines that can write their own computing code or algorithms without human intervention will quickly lead to code that is only understood by AI. [...] CISA released its 2023-2024 Roadmap for Artificial Intelligence, which describes the 5 lines of effort the agency will undertake under the Executive Order [...]
statements.context: Opening statement submitted for the record at a House Homeland Security subcommittee hearing on DHS and CISA's role in securing AI.

statements.text: AI is a hot topic today amongst Members of Congress and Americans in every single one of our districts. AI is a broad umbrella term, encompassing many different technology use cases from predictive maintenance alerts in operational technology to large language models like ChatGPT, making building a common understanding of the issues difficult.
statements.venue: Opening statement, House Homeland Security cyber subcommittee hearing on AI executive order

statements.text: The EPA has now withdrawn their March 2023 cybersecurity rule mandating that cybersecurity audits be part of the sanitary surveys; how would the witnesses suggest the Government provide water systems with the support, both financially and systematically, needed to address the cybersecurity challenges immediately facing water systems?
statements.context: House Subcommittee on Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Protection hearing on operational technology security in the water sector.

statements.text: AI has the potential to replace human discretion in decision making with algorithmic decision making in instances that introduce new and significant risks to national security and the rights of Americans. [...] If implemented with transparency and accountability, with well-defined and enforced civil rights protections and safety standards, with good governance and the public interest in mind, and with worker engagement—AI has the potential to provide valuable tools for how Americans will work.
statements.context: Written statement of the International Federation of Professional and Technical Engineers (IFPTE) submitted for the record of a House Homeland Security Committee hearing on the cyber workforce gap, chaired by Rep. Garbarino.

statements.text: As TTPs evolve, including those involving AI-enabled exploits, supply chain compromises, and manipulation of operational technology systems, there may be ambiguity about whether certain cyber threat indicators or defensive measures are covered. [...] Congress should consider modernizing the definitions within the statute to explicitly account for emerging threats, including indicators related to ransomware campaigns, AI anomalies, and software component tampering.
statements.context: Written hearing responses submitted for the record before the House Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Protection Subcommittee on reauthorizing the Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act of 2015.

statements.text: we are looking at regulating AI and it has now been brought up to me twice in the last week how nobody is doing a cybersecurity review of what Congress is contemplating when we are talking about regulating AI. [...] Nobody is looking at whether the AI product is going to have data protections or cybersecurity built into it.
statements.context: House hearing on leveraging technology for cybersecurity and compliance, where Representative Garbarino questions witnesses about integrating security reviews into AI legislation.

statements.text: But I will say quickly though there is going to be a tension between rapid model adoption and whatever kind of security protocol we put into place. [...] So I would just say whatever we do, maybe think in terms of incentivizing the kind of security but not delaying the adoption of these models.
statements.context: Remarks by Rep. Andrew Garbarino during a House Homeland Security Subcommittee hearing on technology and cybersecurity compliance.

statements.text:
Today, I chaired an @HomelandGOP Subcommittee on Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Protection hearing on securing AI to strengthen U.S. cybersecurity.

As adversaries weaponize this technology, we must ensure it’s built and deployed securely to protect our infrastructure and stay ahead of emerging threats.

WATCH: https://t.co/4aGFDlXGDm

However, we must be clear-eyed: while AI bolsters our productivity and security, our adversaries also hope to use the technology for their own gain. Our nation’s adversaries increasingly weaponize AI to scale and more quickly develop attacks against American citizens, businesses, and government entities.
statements.venue: Opening statement, House Homeland Security cyber subcommittee hearing on securing AI

statements.text: While our adversaries leverage AI to improve their ability to target the United States, we must use it to secure and defend our technological advancements and infrastructure. AI is our competitive advantage—one that will keep us ahead of our adversaries, as long as we build and use it securely.
statements.venue: Opening statement, House Homeland Security cyber subcommittee hearing on securing AI

statements.text: I’m encouraged by continued developments in artificial intelligence to support federal homeland security efforts. This technology can serve as both a force multiplier and efficiency measure, better directing efforts and resources during large-scale events.

``(1) Artificial intelligence.—The term `artificial intelligence' has the meaning given such term in section 5002(3) of the National Artificial Intelligence Initiative Act of 2020 [...] information systems or operational technology systems, including either or both of such systems using artificial intelligence, maintained, owned, [...]
statements.context: Floor debate in the House of Representatives on a motion to suspend the rules and pass H.R. 5078, the PILLAR Act, reauthorizing CISA's state and local cybersecurity grant program.

statements.text: We’ve seen AI being used by the bad guys in cyberattacks for years now, but this was the most aggressive use, and it is very concerning that it could just get worse. So, one thing I’ve been talking about with the private sector, you know, 85 percent of our critical infrastructure is held by the private sector, controlled by the private sector, is if the bad guys are going to be using AI to attack us, we should be using AI…in our cyber defenses because it’s not going to be possible to fight this aggressive use of AI and cyberattacks by just human intervention and defense alone. So, we have to step up our game.
statements.venue: Bloomberg 'Balance of Power' interview, via House Homeland Security Committee release

statements.text: Are there any—and maybe it is the States but are there any regulatory structures that are currently standing in the way of AI delivering on the promise to expand access to affordable housing?
statements.context: Asked during a House Financial Services Committee hearing on AI innovation in financial services.

statements.text: Mr. Stevens, as AI enters mortgage lending, should we extend existing Federal financial services regulatory frameworks to cover AI?
statements.context: Speaking at a hearing on AI innovation in financial services, the lawmaker asks a witness about extending federal regulatory frameworks to AI in mortgage lending.

statements.text:
Glad to help co-moderate @TechNetUpdate Day on the Hill this week. 

We had a strong conversation about AI, emerging technology, and what it means for jobs, national security, and our economic competitiveness.

This space is moving quickly and Congress has to keep up. We need smart policies that support innovation while protecting American workers and keeping the U.S. ahead.

The Chinese Communist Party is trying to turn America’s AI breakthroughs into Beijing’s strategic advantage. Through adversarial model distillation and the rapid global distribution of PRC-developed models, China is working to undercut U.S. leadership, weaken trusted American alternatives, and embed CCP-aligned technology across the software supply chains our economy and national security depend on.
statements.venue: Press release announcing joint investigation with House Select Committee on China

statements.text:
AI is already transforming the way we work, defend our country, and protect critical infrastructure. We must ensure America leads in innovation while putting the right safeguards in place. 

Thanks @PunchbowlNews for the great conversation. https://t.co/ubXMWghpJZ
statements.quoted:
Anthropic brought their most advanced AI into a congressional hearing room — and demonstrated how it could find security vulnerabilities in a bank's systems.

@RepGarbarino explains why they did it, and what it means for the AI debate in Washington. https://t.co/VrU5PrDHxE

statements.text: We can’t continue to defend at human speed when they’re going to be using computer speed to attack us. It’s just not going to work out. We need to be able to defend at computer speed, and having access to models like Mythos to shore up our systems before there’s an attack is very important. Anybody that would sit and go through and watch the demonstration of these models would understand that very clearly––that we need to act soon.
statements.venue: Punchbowl News 'Fly Out Day' interview, via House Homeland Security Committee release

statements.text: I think federal pre-emption is something that should be part of it… I don’t think we should slow down. I think we should be involved in testing. I think guardrails have to be in place… With these new AI models, you have the ability to not just learn how to do it, but to tell it to do it for you.
statements.venue: Punchbowl News 'Fly Out Day' interview, via House Homeland Security Committee release

statements.text: My number one concern, especially when it comes to AI and these models, is cybersecurity…
statements.venue: Punchbowl News 'Fly Out Day' interview, via House Homeland Security Committee release

statements.text: Since then, we’ve passed 20 Committee bills through the House, strengthened security for major events like the World Cup, and led efforts to address emerging threats from AI, cyberattacks, terrorism, and more. https://t.co/7T5CvC2GnE

As Chairman of @HomelandGOP, a major part of my job is making sure we understand emerging threats before they become bigger problems. That includes the dangers posed by jailbroken AI models and the ways this technology can be exploited by bad actors.

Technology is moving quickly, and we need to make sure our homeland security efforts are keeping pace to protect Americans and our communities.
statements.quoted: Glad to be joined by @SpeakerJohnson and @SteveScalise this week as we demonstrated some of the technology being used and evaluated across our homeland security mission. https://t.co/x1Nn0xSCl2

statements.text:
As Chairman of the House Committee on Homeland Security, I’m focused on making sure we stay ahead of emerging threats to our country.

My latest report examines how AI is changing the threat landscape and what we need to do to keep Americans safe.

Read more in Newsday: https://t.co/4fXiMl3MEP
